object_types.name: Vendor
object_types.definition: A supplier onboarded into the supplier master, identified by a vendor number

source_references.excerpt: The vendor record. It's the thing in the supplier master.
Oh. Vendor number. Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created.

object_types.name: Tax ID

object_types.name: Vendor Status
object_types.definition: The lifecycle status of a vendor

source_references.excerpt: Draft, active, suspended.

object_types.name: Spend Tier
object_types.definition: Procurement's classification of a vendor by spend level

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor has a tier. Bronze, silver, gold.
I'm talking about spend. Gold vendors are the ones we spend real money with

object_types.name: Risk Tier
object_types.definition: Compliance's classification of a vendor by risk level, derived from the risk review

source_references.excerpt: I use low, medium, high.
And I'm talking about risk. Low, medium, high, based on the review

object_types.name: Risk Review

source_references.excerpt: The review is its own record. It has a review ID, because we need to know who signed it and when

ambiguities.description: Whether 'six things' in onboarding is an exact or approximate count, and whether they represent distinct fact types to model (record creation, tax documentation, banking/fraud verification, payment system entry, compliance piece, approval) is unclear -- Dana hedges on the count and only some of these are later detailed.

source_references.excerpt: which is honestly about six different things happening in parallel and not always in the same order
I said six, I don't know that it's exactly six.

ambiguities.description: Three address types (remit-to, ship-from, legal) are mentioned as attributes of a vendor but never modeled in detail -- unclear if these should be separate fact types/value types or a single Address object type with a role, and how they relate to accuracy issues ('frequently wrong').

source_references.excerpt: Address, though we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong.

ambiguities.description: Approval of onboarding 'depends on how much we're planning to spend' is mentioned but never elaborated -- unclear what fact type or constraint (e.g., approval thresholds, approver roles) should capture this.

source_references.excerpt: And then somebody has to actually approve it, which depends on how much we're planning to spend.

ambiguities.description: The known duplicate-vendor problem (same tax ID, unmerged duplicate records) is acknowledged as a real data quality issue affecting compliance's ability to see aggregate exposure, but is explicitly out of scope; it's unclear whether this should be modeled as a constraint violation to detect or left entirely unmodeled.

source_references.excerpt: We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together, or we've onboarded the same company twice by accident and nobody's merged them.
The duplicates are also a compliance problem, for what it's worth. If we've got the same entity twice we can't see aggregate exposure.

ambiguities.description: Terminology collision: both procurement and compliance call their classification 'tier', causing confusion. The transcript resolves that in the system these are two separate fields (Spend Tier, Risk Tier), but it's unclear if this naming collision should also be reflected/flagged in the conceptual model itself (e.g., via aliases warning) since 'half the room hears different things' when the plain word 'tier' is used.

source_references.excerpt: And you both call it "tier." ... We both call it tier and it causes genuine chaos... We've asked people to say spend tier and risk tier. Nobody does.

ambiguities.description: Whether a review's 'current' flag is a formally system-modeled attribute or an inferred/derived state is ambiguous -- Raj says 'at most one is the current one' but it's unclear if this is an explicit field on Risk Review or purely a business rule about review sequencing.

source_references.excerpt: A vendor accumulates review records over time. At most one is the current one. Being active requires a current signed-off review.
The review is its own record. It has a review ID, because we need to know who signed it and when, and auditors ask. It's not a checkbox on the vendor.

ambiguities.description: The 'preferred vendor' flag maintained informally in Mei's spreadsheet is explicitly declared out of scope/ad hoc by both Mei and the facilitator, but it represents a real business behavior (choosing among multiple vendors supplying the same thing) that is not modeled -- flagged here rather than incorporated as a fact type per facilitator's own instruction.

source_references.excerpt: There's a column called "preferred." It means if two vendors can supply the same thing, buy from this one. It's not in the system anywhere. It's just my column.
It's ad hoc. Don't model it.

ambiguities.description: The unresolved question of what happens to in-flight purchase orders when a vendor is suspended (halt immediately vs. a proposed 'run-off' state) is explicitly parked as an undecided policy matter, not yet a modelable rule or additional status value; this is a genuine open item rather than a captured constraint.

source_references.excerpt: If we suspend a vendor... what happens to the purchase orders already in flight? My position is that everything halts immediately.
Then we need a middle state. Something like run-off -- existing POs complete, no new ones can be raised.
Parking it explicitly: what happens to in-flight purchase orders when a vendor is suspended is undecided.

ambiguities.description: Final edge case: the facilitator's read-back initially stated 'Every vendor has a risk review,' which Raj corrected to apply only to active vendors, with draft vendors having none. This nuance (mandatory-but-conditional on status, rather than unconditionally mandatory) is a subtle constraint-scoping issue that could easily be mis-modeled as a simple mandatory role on Vendor rather than a conditional/subtype-like rule tied to Vendor Status = active.

source_references.excerpt: A vendor is identified by a vendor number... Every vendor has a risk review.
Every _active_ vendor has a current signed-off review. A draft vendor has no review at all -- that's the normal case, that's what draft means.
